title: The 2026 Midterms Explained: How Congress Flipped, and What Changes Now
alt_titles: Why Democrats Won Both Chambers in 2026
Divided Government Is Back: What the Midterms Mean
The 2026 Midterms: What a Democratic Congress Can and Can't Do
description_summary: On 3 November 2026, Democrats won control of both the Senate and the House. This explainer covers what was at stake, the key results, why voters swung according to the AP Voter Poll, how each party explains it, and what a Democratic Congress can and cannot do with a Republican president. Results as of 9 November 2026; some races are still being counted.

scenes.narration: On the night of 3 November 2026, a Democrat won a Senate race in Texas. No Democrat had won a statewide race there in thirty two years. By the end of the night, Democrats had also won Senate seats in Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina. Within hours, the AP reported they had taken control of the Senate.

panels.caption: Texas: James Talarico wins a Senate seat.

scenes.narration: A few days later, the House followed. For the first time since President Trump returned to office, his party had lost both chambers of Congress. So what happened, why did voters swing, and what can the new Congress actually do? This is the story as of 9 November 2026, with some races still being counted.

Midterms happen halfway through a president's four year term. In 2026, all 435 seats in the House were up for election, along with 35 of the 100 Senate seats. Voters also chose 39 governors, and decided around a hundred ballot measures across 37 states.

Going in, Republicans controlled both chambers. They held the Senate fifty three to forty seven, and had a narrow majority in the House. History was not on their side. The president's party usually loses seats in a midterm. According to Northeastern University researchers, the average swing against it is about twenty five House seats.

panels.label: House seats the president's party loses, on average
The president's party
panels.caption: Midterms usually punish the party in power.

scenes.narration: The maps had also changed. Several states redrew their House districts in the middle of the decade, including Texas, Missouri and North Carolina. California did the same through a ballot measure called Proposition 50. Some analysts expected those new maps to help Republicans. In the end, the swing to Democrats was larger than the map changes.

panels.caption: New district maps in several states.

panels.title: PROPOSITION 50
panels.caption: California redrew its map by ballot.

scenes.narration: In the Senate, Democrats flipped seven Republican held seats, according to the AP. They were Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown returned to the Senate, defeating Senator Jon Husted. In Maine, Senator Susan Collins conceded to Troy Jackson.

panels.title: Seven Senate flips
panels.caption: Seven Republican held seats flip, the AP reports.

scenes.narration: Several of those wins broke long records. In Kansas, Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat to win one of the state's Senate seats since 1932. Democrats held their own seat in Georgia, where Jon Ossoff won re-election. By 7 November, CBS News reported that Democrats would hold at least fifty four Senate seats in January.

panels.label: last time Kansas elected a Democratic senator

scenes.narration: The House moved even further. Democrats needed a net gain of only three seats for a majority. By Saturday 7 November, the AP count had them at more than two hundred and fifty seats. That is well past the 218 needed to control the chamber. About twenty House races were still being counted.

There were firsts too. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black woman to serve as a US state governor. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds became the state's first Black governor. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim elected to the Senate.

Some races are still too close to call. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads Senator Dan Sullivan by a few hundred votes, with about three quarters counted. If nobody passes fifty percent, Alaska's ranked choice count begins on 18 November.

panels.caption: Alaska's ranked choice count, if needed.

scenes.narration: In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom leads Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by about two and a half thousand votes. Late mail and affidavit ballots are still being checked. Her campaign said it would see this through to the very end. In Kansas, the race for governor has triggered a hand count audit.

panels.text: We will see this through to the very end!

scenes.narration: So why did voters swing so hard? The AP Voter Poll surveyed about eighty thousand voters. About four in ten said the economy was the top issue facing the country. Roughly three in ten said the state of democracy. Only about one in ten named immigration or healthcare.

Views of the president mattered. About six in ten voters disapproved of how President Trump was handling the job. About four in ten said they voted to express opposition to him. Just under two in ten said they voted to express support. Roughly four in ten said he was not a factor.

panels.label: disapproved of the president's handling of the job

panels.caption: Many said he was not a factor.

scenes.narration: Some groups shifted sharply. About seven in ten voters under thirty backed the Democrat in their House race. In 2024, the youngest voters were roughly split between Trump and Kamala Harris. Hispanic voters moved too. About a third backed the Republican in their House race, down from roughly four in ten who voted for Trump in 2024.

Then there was the war with Iran, which began in February and pushed up petrol prices. Vice President JD Vance said the reason we lost is the war. President Trump said Iran was a piece of it, but he defended the decision. He said he did the right thing, and would have done it again.

panels.label: Oil disrupted
panels.caption: The Iran war pushed up petrol prices.
Vance: "the reason we lost is the war".

bubble.text: I did the right thing. I would have done it again.

scenes.narration: The two parties tell this story differently. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries called it a change election. Senate leader Chuck Schumer called it a generational remake of the Senate map. Democrats point to cost of living and what they call a need for Congress to check the president.

panels.caption: Schumer: "a generational remake of the Senate map".

scenes.narration: Republicans offer other explanations: the war, prices, and the quality of their candidates. Some Republicans were blunt about it. Senator John Cornyn wrote in the Wall Street Journal that Republicans forgot how to win elections. President Trump said that if he had been on the ballot, his party would have won. He also said Democrats did a good job, and that he was absolutely willing to accept the results.

left_items: Voters want a check on power
right_items: Trump was not on the ballot

panels.caption: Cornyn: Republicans "forgot how to win elections".
Trump: "If I was on the ballot, we would have won."

scenes.narration: Some experts warn against reading too much into it. Northeastern's Martha Johnson said the results are not a clear endorsement of the Democratic policy agenda. Even one of the new senators sounded a warning. Adam Hamilton of Kansas said the wave could be one and done if Democrats do not focus on helping people.

panels.caption: A vote against one side, or for the other?

scenes.narration: The shock has already changed Washington. Speaker Mike Johnson says he will not run to lead House Republicans in the next Congress. Several Republican senators want to delay their own leadership vote. At the White House, Stephen Miller has been named chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

panels.caption: Speaker Johnson will not seek the top Republican job.

scenes.narration: Here is the key point. From January, America will have divided government. A Republican president, and a Congress run by Democrats. That does not hand Democrats the power to pass whatever they want. But it does hand them the power to block, to investigate, and to control the money.

Start with new laws. Any bill Congress passes needs the president's signature. Trump has already said he has the power of the veto. To override it, Congress needs a two thirds vote in both chambers. In the Senate, most bills also need sixty votes to get past a filibuster. Democrats will have about fifty four. So on most laws, they will still need some Republican votes.

panels.label: of both chambers to override a veto
Senate votes to beat a filibuster

scenes.narration: But committees are different. Democrats will chair every committee in both chambers. They can hold hearings and issue subpoenas. Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has already promised serious investigations. Republican Congressman Thomas Massie has said he plans articles of impeachment against Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth unless he resigns.

The Senate also confirms the president's nominees, from cabinet members to federal judges. A Democratic Senate can slow or reject them. And Congress controls government funding. That gives Democrats leverage over spending, including money for the Iran war.

President Trump says he will work with Democrats over his last two years, but will not hesitate to use his veto. He has also called the Senate a roadblock. Democrats say their priorities are affordability and accountability. Whether the two sides can agree on anything is the big unknown.

So what should you watch? On 13 November, the deadline for affidavit ballots in Mississippi. On 18 November, Alaska's ranked choice count, if it is needed. Then come the leadership elections, as both parties choose who will lead them in the House and Senate. Republicans in particular face a contest, with Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan both running.

On 3 January 2027, the new Congress is sworn in. If the House elects him, Hakeem Jeffries would become the first Black Speaker of the House. From then on, for the last two years of this presidency, every big decision in Washington will need both sides. Sources are in the description.
